ssml: <?xml version="1.0"?><speak version="1.0" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2001/10/synthesis" xml:lang="en-US">One link. A whole company shares it.</speak>
<?xml version="1.0"?><speak version="1.0" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2001/10/synthesis" xml:lang="en-US">Lunch hour. Everyone wants it at once.</speak>
<?xml version="1.0"?><speak version="1.0" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2001/10/synthesis" xml:lang="en-US">Something has to slow down.</speak>
<?xml version="1.0"?><speak version="1.0" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2001/10/synthesis" xml:lang="en-US">So, who would you slow down?</speak>
<?xml version="1.0"?><speak version="1.0" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2001/10/synthesis" xml:lang="en-US">Network slicing splits one network into reserved virtual lanes, called slices.</speak>
<?xml version="1.0"?><speak version="1.0" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2001/10/synthesis" xml:lang="en-US">We built a real testbed: seven departments, seven slices, one, one megabit link.</speak>

<?xml version="1.0"?><speak version="1.0" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2001/10/synthesis" xml:lang="en-US">Nine hundred and fifty kilobits are usable, but one thousand four hundred and eighty were promised.</speak>
<?xml version="1.0"?><speak version="1.0" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2001/10/synthesis" xml:lang="en-US">That's normal, like a gym selling more memberships than machines.</speak>
<?xml version="1.0"?><speak version="1.0" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2001/10/synthesis" xml:lang="en-US">Normal networks decide with technical labels, set at install time.</speak>

<?xml version="1.0"?><speak version="1.0" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2001/10/synthesis" xml:lang="en-US">The canteen screens are tagged U R L L C, premium. The regulated quality lab, e M B B, standard.</speak>
<?xml version="1.0"?><speak version="1.0" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2001/10/synthesis" xml:lang="en-US">So the network slows the lab, and protects the lunch menu.</speak>
<?xml version="1.0"?><speak version="1.0" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2001/10/synthesis" xml:lang="en-US">Our software ignores labels and asks business questions.</speak>
<?xml version="1.0"?><speak version="1.0" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2001/10/synthesis" xml:lang="en-US">How critical is it? What does a minute of outage cost?</speak>
<?xml version="1.0"?><speak version="1.0" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2001/10/synthesis" xml:lang="en-US">Factory line, eight thousand four hundred pounds. Canteen screens, fifteen.</speak>
<?xml version="1.0"?><speak version="1.0" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2001/10/synthesis" xml:lang="en-US">Safety rules? Customer impact? How long can it cope? Was it slowed recently?</speak>
<?xml version="1.0"?><speak version="1.0" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2001/10/synthesis" xml:lang="en-US">Then a seven step loop runs every two seconds.</speak>
<?xml version="1.0"?><speak version="1.0" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2001/10/synthesis" xml:lang="en-US">One. Measure real traffic, delay and lost data at the gateway.</speak>
<?xml version="1.0"?><speak version="1.0" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2001/10/synthesis" xml:lang="en-US">Two. Detect: demand over a hundred and two percent of the link, twice in a row.</speak>
<?xml version="1.0"?><speak version="1.0" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2001/10/synthesis" xml:lang="en-US">One spike can't fool it.</speak>
<?xml version="1.0"?><speak version="1.0" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2001/10/synthesis" xml:lang="en-US">Three. Score: each slice gets a business score, zero to a hundred.</speak>
<?xml version="1.0"?><speak version="1.0" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2001/10/synthesis" xml:lang="en-US">Four. Decide. Many small cuts beat one big cut. Harm grows faster than the cut.</speak>

<?xml version="1.0"?><speak version="1.0" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2001/10/synthesis" xml:lang="en-US">One slice cut sixty percent: harm, zero point three six. Six slices cut ten percent: just zero point zero six.</speak>
<?xml version="1.0"?><speak version="1.0" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2001/10/synthesis" xml:lang="en-US">Life-safety slices are never touched. No slice drops below its minimum.</speak>
<?xml version="1.0"?><speak version="1.0" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2001/10/synthesis" xml:lang="en-US">Five. Apply the new speed limits on the gateway.</speak>
<?xml version="1.0"?><speak version="1.0" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2001/10/synthesis" xml:lang="en-US">Six. Restore bandwidth after each recovery window.</speak>
<?xml version="1.0"?><speak version="1.0" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2001/10/synthesis" xml:lang="en-US">Seven. Record a permanent explanation. Nobody can edit or delete it, not even an admin.</speak>

<?xml version="1.0"?><speak version="1.0" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2001/10/synthesis" xml:lang="en-US">In the lunch-hour rush, demand hit one thousand three hundred and sixteen kilobits, with nine hundred and fifty usable.</speak>
<?xml version="1.0"?><speak version="1.0" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2001/10/synthesis" xml:lang="en-US">With a safety margin, it had to free two hundred and fifty one point five kilobits.</speak>
<?xml version="1.0"?><speak version="1.0" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2001/10/synthesis" xml:lang="en-US">Remember our question? The canteen screens took an eighty percent cut.</speak>

<?xml version="1.0"?><speak version="1.0" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2001/10/synthesis" xml:lang="en-US">Office Wi-Fi lost thirty two percent, the warehouse twenty four, C C T V twelve. Patient monitoring was never cut.</speak>

<?xml version="1.0"?><speak version="1.0" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2001/10/synthesis" xml:lang="en-US">Factory and lab: untouched. The gateway enforced it four seconds later, with no button pressed.</speak>
<?xml version="1.0"?><speak version="1.0" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2001/10/synthesis" xml:lang="en-US">What's new? Not slicing, not the sharing maths, but the combination.</speak>
<?xml version="1.0"?><speak version="1.0" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2001/10/synthesis" xml:lang="en-US">Business value, not labels. Small cuts, not one deep cut.</speak>
<?xml version="1.0"?><speak version="1.0" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2001/10/synthesis" xml:lang="en-US">Safety as a hard rule, not a weight.</speak>
<?xml version="1.0"?><speak version="1.0" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2001/10/synthesis" xml:lang="en-US">And it is proved on real traffic, every two seconds recorded.</speak>

<?xml version="1.0"?><speak version="1.0" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2001/10/synthesis" xml:lang="en-US">With arbitration off, the clinic waited half a second. On: twenty three milliseconds, and no loss.</speak>
<?xml version="1.0"?><speak version="1.0" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2001/10/synthesis" xml:lang="en-US">Today the link is real but small: one megabit, shaped in our own software.</speak>

<?xml version="1.0"?><speak version="1.0" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2001/10/synthesis" xml:lang="en-US">Real traffic, measured delay, phones on a hotspot, and the full engine. Four hundred and sixty tests pass.</speak>
<?xml version="1.0"?><speak version="1.0" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2001/10/synthesis" xml:lang="en-US">Next: seven phones measured, kernel shaping, a real five G core, and radio slicing.</speak>

<?xml version="1.0"?><speak version="1.0" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2001/10/synthesis" xml:lang="en-US">When the link is full, it slows down what matters least to the business, in small, fair, safe steps. And it explains every decision.</speak>
